analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take sexual harassment claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, which drew cosponsors from both parties, never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee before the two-year congressional session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers require workers to sign agreements, as a condition of the job, that send any future legal dispute to a private arbitrator instead of a public courtroom. This bill would make those agreements unenforceable when the dispute involves sexual harassment or other sex-based discrimination, letting workers sue in court with a judge or jury. It would not cover race, age, or other kinds of discrimination, and it would leave union contracts alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies that require them to sign pre-dispute arbitration agreements. Under current law, someone facing sexual harassment at work can be forced into a private, often confidential arbitration process with no jury and limited ability to appeal. This bill would give those workers the same access to a public courtroom as other litigants.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any pre-dispute arbitration agreement unenforceable if it requires arbitration of a sex discrimination dispute, meaning a claim rooted in conduct that could form the basis of a Title VII sex discrimination case.
Puts the decision about whether the law applies in the hands of a judge rather than an arbitrator, so the employer cannot have an arbitrator rule on the arbitrator's own authority.
Applies to any dispute or claim arising after enactment, and does not prevent a worker from voluntarily choosing arbitration after a dispute has already arisen.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on arbitration agreements to keep harassment claims out of court. Litigation is more expensive and public than arbitration, and the possibility of a jury verdict and a public record raises the cost of settling or losing harassment cases.

drawbacks.text: Business groups argue that arbitration is faster and less expensive than court litigation for workers as well as employers, and that a wave of sexual harassment lawsuits would raise legal costs, especially for smaller employers.
The bill covers only sex discrimination, so workers facing race, age, disability, or other discrimination would remain subject to forced arbitration under the same contracts.
It would keep collective bargaining agreements untouched, so union members' arbitration channels continue, and it applies prospectively only, doing nothing for claims that arose before enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a worker sexually harassed on the job currently can be contractually barred from ever seeing a courtroom, and this bill would end that for sex-based claims. The main costs are higher litigation expenses for employers and potentially slower, more public resolution of some disputes, which is partly the point. The narrow scope, covering sex but not other discrimination, is a fair criticism, but it reflects this bill being the first slice of a larger issue rather than a design flaw that cancels the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever scheduled it for a hearing or a vote before the session expired.

narrative.text: Representative Cheri Bustos introduced the bill with three original cosponsors across party lines, including Representatives Stefanik, Jayapal, and Griffith.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, February 28, 2019.
On April 8, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where it stayed.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded in the House before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use pre-dispute arbitration agreements keep the ability to route sexual harassment claims into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry keeps the dispute volume. Workers facing harassment on the job did not get their day in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping harassment claims in private arbitration

for.name: Rep. Cheri Bustos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end forced arbitration of sexual harassment claims and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Reps. Elise Stefanik, Pramila Jayapal, and Morgan Griffith
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill Republican and Democratic support from day one.

for.name: 5 of 197 House Republicans and 10 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to 15 members split across both parties.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair Jerrold Nadler)
against.role: Committee chair with power to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: The committee received the referral but never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; no further action was recorded.

against.name: Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law leadership
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was assigned
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its April 2019 subcommittee referral without holding a hearing or advancing it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from introduction: the lead sponsor was a Democrat joined by a Republican original cosponsor, and the 15 cosponsors included 10 Democrats and 5 Republicans; no one publicly opposed the bill, but no committee action followed either.

industries.industry: Employers that use mandatory arbitration agreements
industries.note: These employers, from large corporations to gig platforms, use arbitration clauses to keep sexual harassment claims out of court and often confidential. The bill would expose them to public jury trials, raising the cost of harassment claims.

industries.industry: Arbitration and alternative dispute resolution providers
industries.note: Private arbitration firms and arbitrators would lose the workplace sex discrimination caseload that mandatory agreements currently steer to them. Their business depends on the forced-arbitration system the bill targets.
Firms defending employers against harassment claims would face more courtroom litigation and higher defense costs, while plaintiff-side employment firms would gain a larger docket.
